> Station, N.F.E., 1956. The Timber Resource in Massachusetts. Upper

# Context

Timber use in MA steady for 20yr prior to 1950

I n 1952, almost 21 million cubic f e e t of i n d u s t r i a l timber
products and almost 9 m i l l i o n cubic f e e t of fuelwood were c u t
from Massadhusetts forests.

## Annual Cut of Growing Stock

The 1952 output of timber products, almost 30 million cubic feet,
required a cut of about 26 million cubic feet of growing stock (table
2). In addition, some 7 million cubic feet of timber products -- almost
half of this was for fuelwood -- were obtained from cull trees, dead
trees, hardwood limbs, and plant residues. On the other hand, almost 3
million cubic feet of growing stock were cut but were left in the woods
as waste. This logging residue consisted chiefly of volume in upper
stems.

In terms of sawtimber volume, the 1952 cut was 86 million board feet.
All but 5 percent of the sawtimber volume logged was for sawlog
production. Most of the volume not used for sawlogs was made into
pulpwood.

Thus, almost all the wood used by the forst industries is supplied from
the growing stock; fuelwood is the only major product that is derived
chiefly from other materials such as cull trees and sawmill residues.
Less than a third of the volume cut for fuelwood comes from growing
stock.

## The Supply of Standing Timber

### Growth exceeds Cut

In sharp contrast to the 1952 cut of 26 million cubic feet of growing
stock, the net growth was 80 million cubic feet (table 3). The harvest
in 1952 was only one-third of the growth, chiefly because of the poor
quality of the native timber and the relatively limited markets for
hardwood.

The volume of sawtimber also increased during 1952. Although w39 million
board feet were added to timber stands through sawtimber growth, only 86
million board feet were cut. The cut was 62 percent of the board-foot
growth.

Average annual losses due to fire, windthrow, insect and disease damage,
and suppression were deducted to obtain these net-growth estimates. (NO
specific deductions were made in this report for the estimated los of 50
million board feet, mostly whit pine, due to hurricanes Carol and Edna
in 1954. However, mortality was calculated in an average annual basis,
so it includes some allowance for losses of this kind.) The volume of
ingrowth (saplings that become poletimber or poletimber that became
sawtimber during 1952) was included in the net annual growth estimates
(table 4).

```{r, eval = FALSE}
table_5 <- tribble(
~SizeClass, ~SpeciesGroup, ~AnnualCut, ~NetGrowth,
"Sawtimber", "Softwoods", 13879, 21500,
"Sawtimber", "Hardwoods", 5226, 16100,
"Poletimber", "Softwoods", 1602, 3700,
"Poletimber", "Hardwoods", 4987, 39200
) 
```

Forest Growing Stock

Growing stock is the volume of sound wood in the main stems of all
sawtimber and poletimber trees, from a 1-foot stump to a 4-inch top
inside bark. This volume is estimated to be about 1.9 billion cubic feet
(table 7). More than one-half of it (58 percent) is found in poletimber
trees. Since 0.5 billion cubic feet of sound wood -- in cull trees and
hardwood limbs -- are not counted as forest growing stock, all together
there are 2.4 billion cubic feet of sound wood on the commercial forest
land.

Sawtimber Volume

The sawlog portions of sawtimber trees, amounting to 0.6 billion cubic
feet of sound wood, account for one-third of the growing stock. Measured
according to the International ¼-inch rule (which approximates lumber
tally), this material is equivalent to about 2.7 billion board feet.

The average volume per acre of all sawtimber stands in Massachusetts is
3600 board feet per acre. Many of the sawtimber stands contain barely
enough sawtimber (1,500 board feet per acre) to rate as sawtimber
stands. Loggers will not go into forest stands that have so little
sawtimber unless the volume is in softwoods; therefore some of the
sawtimber volume is in sawtimber stands that are not profitable to log
under present conditions. Even more important than this, about 1.2
billion board feet of sawtimber (47 percent of the total) is scattered
through poletimber stands and seedling-and-sapling stands that will be
inoperable for sawtimber for some time to come (table 9).

Thus, only a portion of the sawtimber in Massachusetts is now
merchantable. Less than half of the total board-foot volume is in the
readily acceptable species, located in stands that loggers regard as
operable timber. These operable stands are widely scattered about the
state, and many are small in area.

p 12:
For sawtimber trees, the cut is much closer to growth. In terms of
sawtimber volume, the board-foot cut of softwoods is more than 90
percent of the net annual growth, but the board-foot cut of
hardwoods is only one-third of their growth.

Condition of the Forests

There are almost 3.3 million acres of forest land in Massachusetts
(table 12). Practically all o fit is commercial forest land. About
18,000 acres of productive forest land are reserved from timber cutting,
mostly in watersheds and state county reservations. Another 11,300 acres
of forest land are classed as unproductive, chiefly because of poor soil
conditions.

Oak forests occupy two-fifths of commercial forest land. They average
only 460 board feet per acre. Other forest types average 860 board feet
per acre.

White pine are scattered through hardwood stands. Stands in which white
pine dominates cover one-seventh of the commercial forest land. White
pine and other softwood stands average better than 1,300 board feet per
acre.

10, 12, and 14 inches are "small" sawtimber diameter classes

Over half of softwood sawtimber volume is in small diameter classes Over
60 percent of hardwood sawtimber volume is in 12 and 14 inch classes

growing stock is 6-inch and larger diameter classes

85 percent of the private ownerships are less than 100 acres in size.
They account for 38 percent of the State's commercial forestland. Only
five holdings are larger than 5,000 acres.

Forest type definitions in the appendix.

## Minimum Cutting Practice Standards

Possibly from:

> Massachusetts Forest Cutting Practices Act of 1943 (enacted as Chapter 539 of the Acts of 1943, codifying M.G.L. Chapter 132, §§ 40–46)

These standards required:

- If an area was clearcut, leave seed trees (4 - 6 thrifty, well-distributed
seed trees per acre of commercial species at least 10-12 inches DBH), UNLESS
adequate regeneration is already established
- Minimum diameter cutting guides by forest type
- Young growth protection - avoid unnecessary damage to saplings,
poles, and seed trees
- Slash disposal - clear back from property boundaries, public roads,
and water bodies to minimize fire risk

Minimum DBH

- Eastern White Pine - 12

  - Except in poor stands or dense pine-hemlock mixes, when it was 10
  
- Oak, Northern Hardwoods - 12 to 14

  - "high value" - northern red oak, sugar maple, white ash, black cherry - it's 14
  
Residual Stand Density

- 200 - 300 vigorous saplings and poles 2-6 dbh

- guidelines "advise against" removing more thatn 35% - 50% of the
  merchantable volume in a single partial cutting cycle
  
in 1982, these went from advisory to mandatory


# MINHARV

Specifies the minimum acceptable harvest standards for board-foot
volume, merchantable cubic-foot volume, Ba/acre, or total cubic foot
volume. Accumulated removals across all thinnings in a cycle must exceed
the standards or no thinnings will be implemented.

# Board Feet

When do stands reach the board-foot minimum?

There are two situations:

1.  The number of board feet in softwoods exceeds 1500/acre
2.  The total number of board feet in the stand exceeds some other
    mininum

The board-foot minimum for hardwood or mixed stands is TBD

## Meets or Exceeds

Sadly, FVS_Stats_Species only contains info for the initial stand, so we
need to build it from the treelist.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
meets_or_exceeds <- cficop_none_treelist |>
  mutate(SpeciesFIA = as.integer(SpeciesFIA)) |>
  left_join(
    species_crosswalk |>
      select(SPCD, HARD_SOFT),
    by = join_by(SpeciesFIA == SPCD)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    size_class = size_class(DBH, HARD_SOFT)
  ) |>
  group_by(Year, StandID, HARD_SOFT, size_class) |>
  summarize(
    BoardFeet = sum(BdFt * TPA),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

```{r, eval = FALSE}
meets_or_exceeds |>
  filter(Year < 2021) |>
  filter(size_class == "sawtimber") |>
  mutate(meets = BoardFeet > 1500) |>
  ggplot(aes(Year, fill = HARD_SOFT)) +
  geom_bar(position = "dodge") +
  theme_bw() +
  ggtitle("CFI plots with >1500 Board Feet/Acre of Sawtimber") +
  ylab("Number of Plots") +
  labs(fill = NULL)
```

Let's look just at white and red pine, which are preferred for harvest.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
meets_or_exceeds <- cficop_none_treelist |>
  mutate(SpeciesFIA = as.integer(SpeciesFIA)) |>
  left_join(
    species_crosswalk |>
      select(SPCD, HARD_SOFT),
    by = join_by(SpeciesFIA == SPCD)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    size_class = size_class(DBH, HARD_SOFT),
    wood_type = case_when(
      SpeciesFIA == 125 | # Red Pine
        SpeciesFIA == 129 ~ # Eastern White Pine
        "Red/White Pine",
      SpeciesFIA == 833 | # Northern Red Oak
        SpeciesFIA == 318 | # Sugar Maple
        SpeciesFIA == 541 | # White Ash
        SpeciesFIA == 762 ~ # Black Cherry
        "High-Value Hardwood",
      HARD_SOFT == "SOFTWOOD" ~ "Other Softwood",
      .default = "Other Hardwood"
    ),
    big_enough = if_else(
      wood_type == "High-Value Hardwood", DBH >= 14, DBH >= 12
    )
  ) |>
  filter(big_enough) |>
  group_by(Year, StandID, wood_type) |>
  summarize(
    BoardFeet = sum(BdFt * TPA),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

```{r, eval = FALSE}
meets_or_exceeds |>
  filter(Year < 2021) |>
  mutate(meets = BoardFeet > 1500) |>
  filter(meets) |>
  ggplot(aes(Year, fill = wood_type)) +
  geom_bar(position = "dodge") +
  theme_bw() +
  ggtitle("CFI plots with >1500 Board Feet/Acre of Sawtimber") +
  ylab("Number of Plots") +
  labs(fill = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1970, 2020, 10))
```

```{r, eval = FALSE}
meets_or_exceeds |>
  filter(Year < 2021) |>
  mutate(meets = BoardFeet > 3000) |>
  filter(meets) |>
  ggplot(aes(Year, fill = wood_type)) +
  geom_bar(position = "dodge") +
  theme_bw() +
  ggtitle("CFI plots with >3000 Board Feet/Acre of Sawtimber") +
  ylab("Number of Plots") +
  labs(fill = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1970, 2020, 10))
```

We can't harvest more in a year than local sawmills can handle. NERS
Figure 1 covers this; the approximate location of the Quabbin watershed
is outlined in blue. Many sawmills are adjacent to the
watershed, and show a capacity for 2,000+ thousand board feet
per year (over 2 million board feet per year). At 1500 bd ft/acre,
we can harvest 1300 acres/year without exceding sawmill capacity.

```{r, eval = FALSE, echo = FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics("data/images/NERS Figure 1.png")
```

# Map

## Plot Harvest Year

```{r, eval = FALSE}
plot_harvest_year <- meets_or_exceeds |>
  filter(wood_type == "Red/White Pine" | wood_type == "High-Value Hardwood") |>
  filter(BoardFeet > 1500) |>
  group_by(StandID) |>
  slice_min(Year) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(MasterPlotID = as.numeric(StandID)) |>
  select(MasterPlotID, HarvestYear = Year)
```

## Plot Used

Map all the plots, including the ones not used in this study.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
plots_for_map <- tblDWSPCFIPlotsComplete |>
  filter(Watershed == 1) |>
  filter(!is.na(GPSLatitude) & !is.na(GPSLongitude)) |>
  select(MasterPlotID, lat = GPSLatitude, lon = GPSLongitude) |>
  left_join(
    cfigro_plot |>
      filter(INV_YEAR == 1970) |>
      mutate(plot_used = "Used") |>
      select(STAND_ID, plot_used),
    by = join_by(MasterPlotID == STAND_ID)
  ) |>
  left_join(
    plot_harvest_year,
    by = join_by(MasterPlotID)
  ) |>
  replace_na(list(plot_used = "Not Used")) |>
  terra::vect()

plots_ext <- plots_for_map |>
  terra::buffer(2 * 1000) |>
  terra::ext()

```

## Basemap Tiles

Download a pretty background for the map

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# Download tiles
basemap_filename <- file.path(
  "data/raw/osm",
  paste0("basemap_quabbin.tif")
)
if (!file.exists(basemap_filename)) {
  apikey = read_lines(file.path("config", "carto_apikey.txt"))
  
  basemap_area <- plots_ext |>
    terra::vect(crs = plots_for_map)
  
  basemap_web <- basemap_area |>
    terra::project(crs("epsg:3857")) |> # use webmercator
    st_as_sf()
  
  # For zoom levels, see:
  # https://wiki.openstreetmap.org/wiki/Zoom_levels
  basemap <- maptiles::get_tiles(
    basemap_web,
    provider = "Esri.WorldTopoMap",
    apikey = apikey,
    # let get_tiles() work out the zoom automatically
    zoom = 11,
    crop = TRUE
  )
  
  terra::writeRaster(basemap, basemap_filename, overwrite = TRUE)
} else {
  basemap <- terra::rast(basemap_filename)
}
```

## The Map

```{r plot grow-only plots, eval = FALSE}
ggplot() +
  geom_spatraster_rgb(data = basemap) +
  geom_polygon(
    data = map_data("state", "Massachusetts"),
    aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group),
    color = "black", fill = "transparent"
  ) +
  geom_spatvector(
    data = plots_for_map,
    # Color will be the year it gets harvested in baseline
    aes(color = HarvestYear, shape = plot_used),
    size = 1.5
  ) +
  scale_shape_manual(
    name = "Plot Status",
    values = c(
      "Used" = 19, # circle
      "Not Used" = 1 # open circle
    )
  ) +
  annotation_scale(
    location = "br",
    pad_x = unit(0.45, "cm"),
    pad_y = unit(0.1, "cm")
  ) +
  annotation_north_arrow(
    location = "tr",
    width = unit(1, "cm"),
    pad_x = unit(-0.25, "cm"),
    pad_y = unit(0.1, "cm"),
    style = north_arrow_minimal,
    which_north = "true"
  ) +
  coord_sf(
    xlim = c(plots_ext$xmin, plots_ext$xmax),
    ylim = c(plots_ext$ymin, plots_ext$ymax),
    crs = crs(plots_for_map)
  ) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(
    option = "turbo",
    na.value = "gray75",
    begin = 0.1
  ) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 9) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = -30, hjust = 0, vjust = 1)) +
  ggtitle("CFI plots 1957 Baseline Harvest") +
  xlab("Longitude") +
  ylab("Latitude")
```

```{r, eval = FALSE}
ggsave("cfi_baseline_1957.png", dpi = 600, width = 10, units = "cm")
```

## Plots that never make it

```{r, eval = FALSE}
plots_for_map |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  filter(is.na(HarvestYear))
```

First one is plot 10163

```{r, eval = FALSE}
meets_or_exceeds |>
  filter(StandID == "10163")
```

Yeah, never makes it to the 1500 board foot high-value threshold.
Probably these plots would be harvested if they're adjacent to a high-
value plot and they have >1500 board feet of lower value wood.

# Acres

p28 "Most of these [private] ownerships--particularly those of 100 acres
or more--can be managed for timber production with little or not conflict
with other owner interests."

So probably harvest 100 acres minimum, when they get to 1500 bd ft/acre,
which is 150,000 bs ft per harvest (minimum).

Bah, let's ignore acres for now, and just harvest plots.

# Harvest Schedule

Most of the harvest (THIN) keywords don't allow species to be specified,
and I need per-species control.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
tribble(
  ~keyword, ~species, ~description,
  "ThinABA", "No", "Thin from Above to Basal Area",
  "ThinATA", "No", "Thin from Above to Trees per Acre",
  "ThinAuto", "No", "Thin Automatically",
  "ThinBBA", "No", "Thin from Below to Basal Area",
  "ThinBTA", "No", "Thin from Below to Trees per Acre",
  "ThinCC", "Yes", "Thin to Canopy Cover",
  "ThinDBH", "Yes", "Thin in DBH Range",
  "ThinHT", "Yes", "Thin in Height Range",
  "ThinMIST", "No", "Thin trees with dwarf Mistletoe",
  "ThinPRSC", "N/A", "Thin by Prescription",
  "ThinPT", "Yes", "Thin by Point",
  "ThinQFA", "Yes", "Thin Quad-Factor Approach",
  "ThinRDEN", "Yes", "Thin to Relative Density (Northwest variant)",
  "ThinRDSL", "Yes", "Thin to Relative Density (Northeast variant)",
  "ThinSDI", "Yes", "Thin to Stand Density Index"
) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

In general, I don't want to do priority by species - if it's a big tree
of a preferred species, I want it removed for wood; if it's a big tree
of a non-preferred species, I want it removed to make room for trees
of preferred species.

I think I'll go simple and ThinATA everything down to 14" DBH. I may
need to play games to keep some trees of each species, but if CUTEFF
is 0.5, that should happen on its own.

Since we are harvesting with 0.5 CUTEFF, and foresters won't harvest
if they can't take <1500 bd ft / acre, we need 3000 bd ft / acre in
order to harvest.

```{targets cficop_bl56_thinata, tar_simple = TRUE}
cficop_bl56_thinata <- cficop_none_treelist |>
  mutate(SpeciesFIA = as.integer(SpeciesFIA)) |>
  mutate(
    wood_type = case_when(
      SpeciesFIA == 125 | # Red Pine
        SpeciesFIA == 129 ~ # Eastern White Pine
        "Red/White Pine",
      SpeciesFIA == 833 | # Northern Red Oak
        SpeciesFIA == 318 | # Sugar Maple
        SpeciesFIA == 541 | # White Ash
        SpeciesFIA == 762 ~ # Black Cherry
        "High-Value Hardwood",
      .default = "Other"
    )
  ) |>
  filter(wood_type == "Red/White Pine" | wood_type == "High-Value Hardwood") |>
  # We're only harvesting 14" and bigger
  filter(DBH >= 14) |>
  # This finds the year when EITHER the valuable softwood or hardwood
  # reaches 1500 bd ft / acre; it's probably valid to harvest when the
  # COMBINED bd ft / acred reaches 1500 bd ft / acre
  group_by(Year, StandID, wood_type) |>
  summarize(
    BoardFeet = sum(BdFt * TPA),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  filter(BoardFeet > 3000) |>
  group_by(StandID) |>
  # First year over 3000 bd ft / acre is the harvest year
  slice_min(Year) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(MasterPlotID = as.numeric(StandID)) |>
  select(MasterPlotID, HarvestYear = Year) |>
  # Harvest in the HarvestYear, and 20 years later
  mutate(
    HarvestPlus20 = HarvestYear + 20,
    HarvestPlus40 = HarvestYear + 40
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(!MasterPlotID, values_to = "HarvestYear") |>
  select(MasterPlotID, HarvestYear) |>
  filter(HarvestYear <= 2020) |>
  mutate(
    TARGET_TPA = 0, # MA Guidelines say 5 per species; since CUTEFF = 0.5, this can be 0
    PERCENT = 0.5, # MA guidelines
    DBH_MIN = 14, # MA Guidelines
    DBH_MAX = 999 # No upper bound
  ) |>
  # For ThinATA, our schema is:
  # STAND_CN, YEAR, TARGET_TPA, PERCENT, DBH_MIN, DBH_MAX
  # Not Implemented: HEIGHT_MIN, HEIGHT_MAX
  # Get STAND_CN
  left_join(
    cfigro_plot |>
      filter(INV_YEAR == 1970) |>
      select(STAND_CN, STAND_ID),
    by = join_by(MasterPlotID == STAND_ID)
  ) |>
  select(
    STAND_CN,
    YEAR = HarvestYear,
    TARGET_TPA,
    PERCENT,
    DBH_MIN,
    DBH_MAX
  ) |>
  # Arrange this for humans to be able to digest
  arrange(STAND_CN, YEAR)
```

# Run FVS

What happens with the baseline scenario as set up by the 1956 NERS
report?

```{targets cficop_bl56}
tar_target(
  cficop_bl56,
  {
    timestep <- 10 # years; determined by FVSne variant
    fvsbin_dir <- "~/bin" # TODO: put these in a config file
    fvs_variant <- "FVSne"      # TODO: put these in a config file
    data_dir <- "data/fvs"
    title <- "CFICarbonOffsetProgram"
    mgmt_id <- "BL56"
    project_dir <- file.path(data_dir, paste0("FVS_", title, "_", mgmt_id))
    if (!dir.exists(project_dir)) {
      dir.create(project_dir)
    }
    
    fvs_run(
      fvsbin_dir = fvsbin_dir,
      fvs_variant = fvs_variant,
      project_dir = project_dir,
      fiadb = NULL,
      title = title,
      mgmt_id = mgmt_id,
      stands = cfigro_plot |>
        # Filter out the 6 plots that do not get a sibling
        semi_join(
          cficop_plot_sibling,
          by = join_by(STAND_ID == MasterPlotID)
        ) |>
        mutate(
          ASPECT = if_else(SLOPE > 0 & ASPECT == 0, 360, ASPECT),
          # We don't use microplot data, but there are 4x6' radius
          # microplots
          INV_PLOT_SIZE = 385/4
        ),
      trees = cfigro_trees |>
        filter(DIAMETER > 0),
      regen = cficop_dflt_estab,
      harvest = cficop_bl56_thinata,
      num_partitions = fvs_num_partitions,
      partition = fvs_partition,
      random_seed = fvs_randseed
    )
  },
  # iteration = "vector" branches execution for each partition value (see below)
  iteration = "vector",
  # cross() and map() are unparsed targets:: functions here.
  # cross() ensures that every combination of values for its arguments is processed
  # map() distributes each value of its argument to a separate sub-target (branch)
  # so cross(randseed, map(partition)) will run each partition in a separate branch,
  # and each branch will run with each value of randseed
  pattern = cross(fvs_randseed, map(fvs_partition))
)
```
